title: Tiny ancient fossils may reveal an early magnetic navigation system
summary:
Some animals can find their way using Earth’s magnetic field. Now tiny fossils may offer clues about how long this ability has existed.

Researchers studied magnetic fossils dating back 97 million years. They were found in ancient seafloor sediments in the North Atlantic Ocean. The fossils have shapes like spearheads, spindles, bullets and needles. Each is no larger than a bacterial cell.

Scientists think a living organism made these structures, but they do not know which organism it was. Their purpose has also been uncertain.

A team from the University of Cambridge and the Helmholtz Zentrum Berlin made the first three-dimensional images of the magnetic structures inside the fossils. The results suggest that the structures were well suited to detecting both the direction and strength of Earth’s magnetic field.

That information could have helped an ancient animal work out where it was and which way to travel. Navigation means finding your location and your way from one place to another.

Some bacteria already use tiny magnetic particles as internal compass needles. But the fossils studied here are about 10 to 20 times larger than the particles used by bacteria.

Scientists had earlier suggested that these larger structures might have been protective spines. The new magnetic images support a different possibility: navigation. The creature’s identity is still unknown, and the findings may help scientists understand how animals developed the ability to sense Earth’s magnetic field.
